title: SCOT: Single-Cell Multi-Omics Alignment with Optimal Transport

nodes.text: SCOT (single-cell alignment with optimal transport) is an unsupervised algorithm that aligns single-cell multi-omics datasets using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, requiring neither sample-wise nor feature-wise correspondences.
nodes.evidence: single-cell alignment with optimal transport (SCOT), an unsupervised algorithm that uses the Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport to align single-cell multi-omics data sets

nodes.text: SCOT constructs a k-NN graph per domain, computes graph distance matrices to capture intra-domain geometry, finds a probabilistic coupling minimizing the discrepancy between the intra-domain distance matrices, and aligns via barycentric projection.
nodes.evidence: SCOT achieves this by constructing a k-NN graph for each data set... computing graph distance matrices... finds a probabilistic coupling matrix that minimizes the discrepancy between the intra-domain distance matrices... barycentric projection

nodes.text: Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport compares pairwise distances within each metric space rather than directly comparing data points across spaces, making optimal transport suitable for multimodal alignment where features cannot be directly compared.
nodes.evidence: The Gromov-Wasserstein distance extends optimal transport by comparing distances between data points rather than directly comparing the data points themselves... allows us to work with data from different modalities

nodes.text: SCOT introduces a self-tuning heuristic that uses the Gromov-Wasserstein distance to guide hyperparameter selection in the fully unsupervised setting, without requiring orthogonal correspondence/validation data.
nodes.evidence: SCOT uses a self-tuning heuristic to guide hyperparameter selection based on the Gromov-Wasserstein distance

nodes.text: Unlike Seurat and anchor-based batch-integration methods, SCOT requires no correspondence information among either samples or features, and unlike such methods it performs well in unsupervised settings.
nodes.evidence: SCOT aligns single-cell data sets better than the existing methods without requiring any orthogonal correspondence information

nodes.text: SCOT requires tuning only two hyperparameters (and is robust to one of them), fewer than MMD-MA's three and UnionCom's four, easing tuning in real-world unsupervised settings where no validation correspondences exist.
nodes.evidence: Unlike MMD-MA and UnionCom, SCOT requires tuning only two hyperparameters and is robust to the choice of one

nodes.text: Like UnionCom, SCOT aims to preserve local geometry during alignment, whereas MMD-MA aims to match global distributions in a shared latent space.
nodes.evidence: Like UnionCom, SCOT aims to preserve local geometry when aligning single-cell data... MMD-MA aims to match the global distributions of the data sets in a shared latent space

nodes.text: The Gromov-Wasserstein problem is solved with entropic regularization via projected gradient descent under KL divergence, with projections computed by Sinkhorn iterations, exploiting Peyre's factorization that reduces the tensor product cost to O(nx^2 ny + nx ny^2).
nodes.evidence: Peyre et al. (2016) proposed using a projected gradient descent approach for optimization, where both the projection and the gradient are taken with respect to the Kullback-Leibler divergence. These projections are computed via the Sinkhorn iterations

nodes.text: Across four simulated and two real-world datasets, SCOT aligns data on par with state-of-the-art unsupervised methods (MMD-MA and UnionCom) while being faster and scaling well with increasing sample numbers.
nodes.evidence: SCOT aligns data sets as well as the state-of-the-art methods and scales well with increasing numbers of samples

nodes.text: The Gromov-Wasserstein distance can guide SCOT's hyperparameter tuning in a fully unsupervised setting when no orthogonal alignment information is available, providing a heuristic for hyperparameter selection without validation data.
nodes.evidence: the Gromov-Wasserstein distance can guide SCOTs hyperparameter tuning in a fully unsupervised setting when no orthogonal alignment information is available
